scenes.title: Cold open
on_screen: Title card: Kartik Naach · Nepal · 17th century

scenes.title: Where and when
narration: The dance was started in 1641 AD by King Siddhi Narsingh Malla.
It began as a two-day performance, later expanded by his son Srinivas Malla and grandson Yog Narendra Malla to cover 17 tales of Vishnu over 27 days.

scenes.title: When it is danced
narration: The dance is performed annually in the month of Kartik (October or November) to honor the Hindu god Vishnu through 17 tales.
Today it is a living tradition.

scenes.title: Watch it
narration: Dancers portray Hindu deities including Barahi, Ganesh, Shiva, and Krishna.
They wear colorful clothes and festoons around their necks.
The performance is held in an open-air setting.
scenes.music: diegetic (the video's own sound), underscore under narration

scenes.title: Listen
narration: The performance is accompanied by folk music.
In 2015, the production utilized 45 musicians to support the dance-drama.

scenes.title: The costume and the setting
narration: The dance is performed at the Kartik Dabali in Patan Durbar Square.
Dancers wear colorful costumes and festoons.
A golden window, opened only for the play, is a key feature of the setting.

music_brief.purpose: original soundtrack faithful to the tradition, with documented commercial reuse rights and no recurring royalties
music_brief.rights_rule: A composition brief does not clear an output. Record the provider/model/version, terms and date, input rights, output licence, restrictions and review before release.
music_brief.prompt: Original instrumental composition in the musical world of Kartik Naach (Nepal). New melody, new arrangement: do not quote or imitate any specific recorded song; keep the idiom, the instruments, the pulse and the proportions.

tracks.use: chapters: dance it to the music

rules: Original composition only — no sampling, no melody of any existing recording, no lyrics from any song.
Traditional public-domain tunes may be used only when the profile names them and a public-domain source is on file; otherwise compose new material in the idiom.
Keep the proportions true: the meter, the tempo range and the instrument roles the sources describe.
Label every generated track with the tool, the date and this brief, so provenance is always clear.
